![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096328/assets/b8b8e65b34ae0ae59f7cb291a49fd829cae58555b1fc1f267ac57fc70b63b323.png)

G=⟨0,0,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩.
$$

Current part:

questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $G$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $G$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}G\cdot \,\text{d}S={∬}_{S}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $G=⟨0,0,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $G$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096328/assets/9e894018baf5f651e2d43cb48a324a5470c9061e6da10f666978519b3bff4c7f.png)

Let's consider the flux of $G$ through these two sides.

* Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}G\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-32⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =-xy-32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $G$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}(-xy-32)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(xy+32)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(xy+32)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y+32x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+64)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}+64y]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =-132.\end{aligned}
$$

* Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}G\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $G$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}G\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-132+4 \\  & =-128.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If $G=P\,\text{i}+Q\,\text{j}+R\,\text{k}$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $G$ all exist, then the divergence of $G$ is the scalar field given by

$$
∇\cdot G=\text{div}\,G=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot G & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(0)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(-xy-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =-4z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We have $∇\cdot G=-4z.$
First, we express our triple integral as a repeated integral:

$$
{∭}_{R}∇\cdot G\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}-4z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

Since the domain of integration $R=[0,2]\times [0,2]\times [0,4]$ is a rectangular box, and the integrand can be expressed as $f(x)\cdot g(y)\cdot h(z),$ we can rewrite our repeated integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}-4z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}-2\cdot 2z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{4}2z\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating each integral separately, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{4}2z\,\text{d}z & =-2[x]_{0}^{2}\cdot [y]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{z}^{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =-2\cdot (2-0)\cdot (2-0)\cdot (16-0) \\  & =-128.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: This is equal to the answer found in step 2. This is not a coincidence! It is a consequence of the so-called divergence theorem. If you haven't met the divergence theorem yet, don't worry, you will soon.

                            After some time, the duct's settings are changed. The diagram above shows the flow of air induced at the top of a room in the $xy$-plane around the duct's outlet. The velocity field $F$ in this plane is given by

$$
F=({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{i}-2xy\,\text{j}.
$$

Find the flux of the airflow across the boundary $C$ of the exit of the tube.

*Hint: First check if $F$ is source-free.*

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        The required flux is $\,{∮}_{C}^{}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s\,=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        .
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that, if $F=P\,\text{i}+Q\,\text{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

* $F$ is a source-free vector field.

* $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

* The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

* Flux is path-independent. That is, given two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and end points, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

* There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, for our vector field $F=({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{i}-2xy\,\text{j}$, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy) \\  & =2x-2x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero. Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096328/assets/4693916207540a6453c6c3775824ba577e62fea0a18b07e96f8814901d9ad80e.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,dx+(-2xy)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, by applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2y-(-4y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2y\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

From step 6, we can write this as the following repeated integral:

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

Evaluating the integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =({\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x)\cdot ({\int }_{0}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =x{|}_{0}^{2}\cdot {y}^{2}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(2-0)(4-0) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
